title: Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub
why: If you ever approved a shell command containing an inline password or token in Claude Code, that secret may already be on a public GitHub default branch, and deleting the file does not remove it from git history or forks.
notes: Apiiro scanned 104,185 public copies of .claude/settings.local.json across 103,617 repos; 1,122 copies (about 1.1%) held at least one secret, 1,379 secrets total. The firm did not test whether the keys still work, though one notified company confirmed its key was live.

Mechanism: picking 'Yes, and don't ask again' saves an allow rule. When the prompt offers the exact command rather than a pattern like npm test *, the whole command, including any inline password or token, is stored in plaintext. Reproduced on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Leak persistence: Claude Code adds the file only to the user's global git excludes on first write, never to the project .gitignore, so the protection does not travel and does nothing for already-committed files. A Claude co-authored commit changed the file in 539 of 1,105 traced repos. Every secret-bearing file was still on the default branch as of Monday, there a median 217+ days.

Secret breakdown: over a third open a database directly (379 DB passwords), plus 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 GitHub/GitLab/npm tokens, and 23 AWS keys, spread across 63 organizations. Named standouts (per the researchers): a database vendor's admin-level cloud key and a medical-records DB owner password. Counting git history, forks, committed settings.json, and agent logs raises the total to 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repos.

Scanner blind spot: run without verification, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643 of the 1,122 files; neither caught 215. Misses are passwords typed after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, or mysql -p, which look like ordinary words to key-format scanners.

Of 16 coding agents whose docs were compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save full approved commands in a project file by default. A bug report filed 2025-08-11 and three related reports were all closed by an automated bot as 'not planned' with no reply from Anthropic, per the researchers.
summary: Security firm Apiiro reports that Claude Code's 'Yes, and don't ask again' option can save approved shell commands verbatim, including any inline password, token, or key, into the project file .claude/settings.local.json, and that these secrets have leaked to public GitHub. Of 104,185 public copies scanned, 1,122 held at least one secret, for 1,379 secrets total, including 379 database passwords, 43 SSH logins, 42 Git/npm tokens, and 23 AWS keys across 63 organizations; the researchers did not verify whether the keys still work, though one notified company confirmed a live key. Claude Code adds the file only to a single machine's global git excludes, never to the project .gitignore, so the protection does not travel, and a Claude co-authored commit added the file in 539 of 1,105 traced repos. Deleting the file does not fix the exposure because secrets remain in git history and forks; the recommended order is to rotate every credential first, then clean up. Common scanners miss many cases: run without verification, gitleaks and TruffleHog together failed to flag 215 of the 1,122 files, mostly passwords passed as command flags like PGPASSWORD=. The researchers say Claude Code is the only one of 16 compared agents confirmed to save full approved commands by default, and that four related bug reports since August 2025 were all closed by an automated bot with no Anthropic response.
novelty: quantified secret leakage via Claude Code's auto-approve settings file
audience: developers and security teams using AI coding agents

title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?
why: An AI system settled a weaker form of the 160-year-old Riemann hypothesis that number theorists say carries most of RH's consequences, and it did so by recombining existing tools rather than inventing new math, shifting the open question from "can models do real research math" to "can we verify and read what they produce."
notes: OpenAI announced the quasi-RH proof on October 6, 2026 as part of a large batch of results (the article cites both 377 and 722 papers in different passages). Two versions exist: a September 30 version proving all nontrivial zeros lie between 1/8 and 7/8 (199 pages, formally verified in Lean), and a later ~49-page version proving a weaker 1/12-to-11/12 bound (not yet formally verified).

Mathematicians are concentrating on the shorter 11/12 paper, which Radziwiłł calls the only one of the batch edited by a human; OpenAI declined to say who edited it, responding only that the paper 'is the result of work from everyone at OpenAI.'

Quasi-RH narrows the strip containing the zeta function's nontrivial zeros rather than pinning them to the 1/2 line; Radziwiłł says 'the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH,' spanning number theory, geometry, and theoretical CS.

The proof introduces no new concepts: it synthesizes known ideas, including a 2021 formula by Dunn and Radziwiłł and metaplectic forms Dunn had studied for five years. It realizes Sarnak's decades-old strategy of treating zeta as one member of a function family, using a family Iwaniec narrowly missed in 2002.

Reviewers say the papers are 'horribly written' and would be rejected by any journal; Sarnak is repurposing a course to study it and won't call it 'a Theorem' until humans check every detail. Radziwiłł can now sketch the argument in half a page; private write-ups run 7-13 pages. Experts (Sawin) expect the technique cannot reach the full 1/2 bound, though Bloom notes they'd have said the same about quasi-RH weeks earlier.
summary: Quanta reports that on October 6, 2026, OpenAI announced a claimed proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a weaker form of the Riemann hypothesis that confines the zeta function's nontrivial zeros to a strip narrower than (0,1) rather than fixing them on the real-part-1/2 line. Two versions circulate: a 199-page September 30 proof of a 1/8-to-7/8 bound that was formally verified in Lean, and a shorter ~49-page proof of a weaker 1/12-to-11/12 bound that is not yet verified; mathematicians are focusing on the shorter one, reportedly the only paper in the batch to receive human editing. Number theorists including Radziwiłł, Dunn, Sarnak, and Lichtman largely judge the result correct and call its consequences staggering, since most implications of full RH follow from quasi-RH. The proof's claimed novelty is a synthesis of existing tools, notably metaplectic forms and a 2021 Dunn-Radziwiłł formula, realizing Sarnak's long-standing family-of-functions strategy using a family overlooked since Iwaniec's 2002 work. Reviewers criticize the papers as poorly written by journal standards, and Sarnak withholds the label Theorem pending full human verification. Experts doubt the method extends to the full RH, while cautioning that quasi-RH itself looked out of reach weeks earlier.
novelty: AI proves quasi-Riemann hypothesis via synthesis of known techniques, not new concepts
audience: mathematicians and AI-for-science researchers tracking AI's role in formal proof generation

title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
why: The headline "reads and writes weights to improve Qwen" result actually ran the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems and wrote Python, so treating it as evidence that a model can edit real LLMs by inspection alone misreads what was demonstrated.
notes: The abstract's claim that Astra works 'just by looking at the raw weights' holds only for experiments 1, 2, and 4, on tiny networks of 17K to 172K weights, with no tools and without running the network.

The headline Qwen3.5-0.8B result (MATH-500 7.9% to 48.1%, IFEval up 3x via editing 0.016% of weights) used Python code and ran the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems; every experiment involving a real language model used Python.
The from-scratch MinAtar networks beat PPO-500M only on Breakout (517 vs 25) and lose on Seaquest (53 vs 89) and Asterix (53 vs 55); their weights start at zero, so there is nothing to read.

Fixing a stuck Kinetix car policy (0% to 100%) changed 3.5% of weights in one try after being given one recorded failure episode; spotting a sycophantic Gemma 3 failed with Python alone but passed 3/3 once shown attention patterns across up to 16 texts.

Author's core objection: the post bundles two distinct techniques, direct raw-weight inspection and Python-assisted analysis with model execution, under one narrative; a single technique doing both would imply a deep 'gestalt' capability, which was not tested here.

Author concedes the Python-assisted Qwen work is real engineering that models from a year or two ago would have failed, likening the mixed methods to a stage magician performing the same trick multiple ways.
summary: A critique argues that the "Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen" post conflates fundamentally different techniques under a misleading "just by looking at the raw weights" framing. Using a per-experiment table, the author shows that pure raw-weight reading (floats in context, no tools, no model execution) appears only in three experiments on 17K-172K-weight networks. The headline Qwen3.5-0.8B result, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% by editing 0.016% of weights, instead relied on writing Python and running the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems; every real-LLM experiment used Python. Other results are similarly qualified: the from-scratch MinAtar networks beat PPO-500M only on Breakout, and the Kinetix fix was given a recorded failure episode. The author grants this is genuine work mirroring what human ML engineers do and beyond year-old models, but objects that no single technique was shown to both author small networks from scratch and understand a large existing model, so the post overstates a unified deep capability.
novelty: debunks claim that single technique reads weights to improve models
audience: ML researchers and engineers evaluating interpretability/weight-editing claims

title: The Components of Agent Memory
why: If you build agents, this is Anthropic's working recipe for persistent memory: let the model judge what to save in-session, then run "dreaming" (offline passes over transcripts) to correct wrong notes and build wiki indexes, with measured gains like 13%→48% accuracy as dreaming scaled to 128 sessions.
notes: "Dreaming" is Anthropic's term for offline memory reorganization, borrowed from the Letta/UC Berkeley "sleep-time compute" idea: the agent reflects on logs during idle time to fix mistakes and build new representations. Agent memory is defined narrowly as knowledge saved as re-readable context between sessions, explicitly excluding weight updates, in-context learning, and compaction.

On CL-Bench 1.0 (continual learning via a persisted memory directory across fresh sessions), capability scaled with model: Sonnet 4.6 only generated untested theories, Opus 5 was first to "close the loop" (rules plus evidence plus trap warnings); Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 matched Opus 5. Note the article names unreleased models: Opus 4.7, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 5.5, and "Fable 5."

Pokémon Red salience test: Sonnet 3.7 wrote indiscriminately (413 files across 225 folders, 1 badge) and stalled recombing stale notes; Fable 5 wrote 9 files in 2 folders plus a global.md dashboard and earned 4 badges; Opus 5.5 beat the game. Lesson: don't store what's readable from screen state; store only strategy and tested rules.

Steering finding reversing conventional prompt advice: for stronger models, fixed rules like "record only failures" cut the memory boost (hurt Opus 5 and 4.7); freedom to judge salience won. Steering helped older models most: prompting Sonnet 4.6 to read memory and test theories nearly doubled its score, behavior Sonnet 5 does unprompted (reads memory 9/10 times vs under half for 4.6).

Wiki representation tested on Stainless corpus (~350k files, ~420M tokens, acquired May): across 128 dreaming sessions, grading on 25 questions rose from 13% to 48%. Search+wiki beat search alone (61% vs 53%) and saved ~20k tokens/question. Caveats: on a Harvey LAB brief task the wiki grew larger than the source docs (Borges map analogy) and added nothing; dreaming requires compute and injected top-layer notes burn tokens and can propagate a wrong note into every session.

Instruction-tuning the wiki build mattered: a shared contract-terms table where parallel agents overwrote each other yielded 72% of facts (41/57); giving each contract its own page with verbatim quotes, discovered via a reflect-and-rebuild loop, reached 100%.
summary: Anthropic lays out a taxonomy and set of internal evaluations for agent memory, defined as knowledge Claude saves as re-readable context between sessions (excluding weight updates, in-context learning, and compaction). The central mechanism is "dreaming," offline reflection over session transcripts (derived from the Letta/UC Berkeley "sleep-time compute" concept) used to correct wrong notes, promote notes up a hierarchy, and build wiki representations. Evaluations span CL-Bench 1.0 (where capability to "close the learning loop" improved from Sonnet 4.6 up to Opus 5 and beyond), Pokémon Red (where salience judgment separated profligate Sonnet 3.7 from concise Fable 5), the Stainless document corpus (~420M tokens, where scaling dreaming to 128 sessions raised QA accuracy from 13% to 48% and search+wiki beat search alone), and Harvey LAB legal-brief tasks. Reported lessons: tell Claude what memory is for but not how to use it; fixed salience rules can hurt stronger models; and dreaming's cost and failure modes (bloated wikis, propagated errors, token-heavy context injection) require tuned cadence. All numbers are Anthropic's own self-reported results; some evaluated models (Opus 4.7/5/5.5, Sonnet 5/5.5, Fable 5) are not publicly released, and methodology details are limited to what the post describes.
novelty: Anthropic's taxonomy of agent memory: dreaming, salience prediction, consolidation
audience: engineers building long-horizon AI agents with persistent memory

title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
why: If you use Postman alongside Codex or Claude Code, reopening the desktop app can rewrite your coding agents' config to route API work through Postman, and the installer trusts its own hook without you approving it.
notes: The reporter says opening an existing Postman desktop install (v12.33.4 on macOS) triggered an 'auto-existing-upgrade' that silently added a Codex plugin (1.1.0), a Claude Code plugin (postman@claude-plugins-official v2.0.1, user scope, installed 2026-10-24), a remote MCP connection, and a separate Postman CLI in ~/.local/bin.

The injected hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart hook (matcher startup|clear|compact) printing an instruction to load the postman:api-engineer skill before any non-trivial API task, broader than an explicit user request to use Postman.

installer/src/hosts/codex.ts calls approvePostmanHook(system); codex-hooks.ts computes the hook hash via hooks/list and upserts hooks.state with a trusted_hash via config/batchWrite, which the source comments describe as approving 'only Postman's current hook after installation.'

A commenter reproduced the trust mechanism on Codex CLI 0.162.1: the trusted_hash is a sha256 over sorted-key JSON of the hook's identity, computable offline and writable with a text editor, and it pins the command declaration, not the script file's bytes, so edited scripts still fire. Claude Code 2.1.302 fired settings-file hooks in a non-interactive `claude -p` run with no trust dialog.

The author explicitly does not claim proven data exfiltration and has no clean-machine reproduction; the framing is a consent and trust-boundary violation. The title's 'attempts to share all API data' overstates what the body establishes.

Signal only: GitHub issue #14370 drew 171 Hacker News points and 41 comments plus dozens of reactions; commenters cite corporate-environment risk and allege Postman quietly edited its download page (citing an unchanged 2026-10-26 Wayback snapshot). No maintainer response is recorded in the text.
summary: A GitHub issue reports that reopening an existing Postman desktop app (v12.33.4, macOS) ran an 'auto-existing-upgrade' that silently installed a Codex plugin, a Claude Code plugin (postman@claude-plugins-official v2.0.1), a remote MCP connection, and a Postman CLI, without explicit per-app consent. The core finding is that Postman's installer self-approves its own Codex startup hook: installer/src/hosts/codex.ts calls approvePostmanHook, hashing the hook and writing a trusted_hash into hooks.state via the same hooks/list and config/batchWrite calls the interactive review path uses. The hook injects a SessionStart instruction telling the agent to load the postman:api-engineer skill for any non-trivial API work. A follow-up comment tests the trust mechanism on Codex CLI 0.162.1 and Claude Code 2.1.302, showing the Codex trust record is an offline-computable sha256 that any process in the user account can forge, that it pins the command declaration rather than the script bytes, and that Claude Code fires settings-file hooks in a non-interactive `claude -p` run with no trust dialog. The author explicitly does not claim data exfiltration and has no clean-machine reproduction, framing it as a consent and trust-boundary problem. The issue drew 171 Hacker News points and widespread GitHub reactions, with no maintainer response recorded.
novelty: installer self-approves its own agent hook trust
audience: developers using Postman, Codex, or Claude Code who care about supply-chain/consent boundaries

title: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from
why: When an AI assistant hands you a statistic, there is about a 40% chance you can trace it to a matching study and only a 21% chance the page it cites is the original research, so every number you plan to cite needs a manual two-click follow before it goes anywhere.
notes: Trakkr traced 1,285 statistics sampled from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews, following each citation up to five pages deep. Corrected rates: 40% reached a study saying the same thing, 8% reached the study but with the number or context changed, 40% dead-ended at a locked/gone/silent source, 11% led nowhere.

The AI usually was not fabricating: the cited page carried the figure 82% of the time, but only 21% of cited pages were the original research. More than half were company blogs; news stories and statistics roundups make up most of the rest.

Starting point predicts success: trails beginning at a research firm or government page reached a matching study 61% of the time, versus 37% from a company blog and 35% from a roundup; even research-firm trails failed 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form.

ChatGPT quoted the fewest numbers (1.3 per answer vs Claude's 6.8); the other four assistants clustered at 38-46% sourcing, too close to rank. Agreement was not a quality signal: four stats quoted by all five assistants had no findable study, and of 29 stats quoted by three or more, only 11 were sourced.

On 28 of 71 questions all five answered with a percentage, they produced four or five different figures, with a typical 16-point spread between highest and lowest. Of statistics that reached the study, 17% had drifted; the digits moved only about a quarter of the time, with the rest being changes to what was measured, the year, the source, or who was asked.

Methodology caveat stated in the piece: an AI model judged every trail, a stronger model re-judged 300, and humans re-checked 150 at random with a third check on disagreements. The model alone undercounted sourcing (23% vs the hand-corrected 40%); reported rates carry ranges from both. A separate 300-statistic trace of real Google AI Overviews searches (Sept 25-Oct 25, 2026; 4.4% of 52,930 queries carried a stat) also landed at 40% sourced.
summary: Trakkr asked five AI assistants (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Google AI Overviews) 200 questions requiring a number, then manually walked 1,285 sampled citation trails up to five pages deep, from the cited page to that page's own source. After human-corrected scoring, only 40% of statistics reached a matching original study, another 8% reached the study with the number or context changed, 40% stopped at an unverifiable source, and 11% led nowhere. The assistants were mostly not inventing numbers (the cited page carried the figure 82% of the time), but only 21% of cited pages were the original research; the majority were company blogs, news, or statistics roundups repeating figures without linking back. ChatGPT cited the fewest statistics per answer (1.3 vs Claude's 6.8), while sourcing rates otherwise clustered at 38-46%. Agreement across assistants was not a reliability signal: on 28 of 71 questions all five gave four or five different figures (typical 16-point spread), and four stats quoted by all five had no findable study. The piece recommends following each citation at least twice, checking who was asked and when, and, for publishers, putting method and source on the same page as the number.
novelty: quantified citation-trail audit of AI assistants' cited statistics
audience: engineers/researchers building or evaluating AI search/answer products and RAG citation trust

title: GitLab Security Incident: Attempted Exploitation of CVE-2026-97229
why: If you run GitLab with your own Ruby build instead of GitLab's official packages, patching GitLab to 19.3.5+ does not close CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS 10.0); you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, or 4.0.9, and Alpine's own instance stayed exploitable even after two upgrades until they rebuilt it with patched Ruby.
notes: CVE-2026-97229 is a CVSS 10.0 bug in how GitLab evaluates regex in CI configuration; the root cause is in Onigmo, the regex engine built into Ruby, not in GitLab's own code. GitLab shipped the fix Oct 12 as patches to the Ruby it bundles; upstream Ruby only shipped it Oct 23 in 3.3.13, 3.4.12, and 4.0.9.

The patching trap: Alpine first upgraded to 19.3.4 by mistake instead of the fixed 19.3.5 on Oct 13, then upgraded to 19.3.6 on Oct 22 and remained vulnerable because their container used stock Ruby that never received GitLab's Ruby patch. Fix requires either GitLab's official packages or a patched Ruby version.

Attack mechanics (Oct 20-21): a newly registered account sent crafted CI configs that crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times; in 4 crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also pulled Alpine's GitLab container image, suggesting they were tuning the exploit to the exact build.

Alpine self-reports no evidence of code execution (timing probes showed no delays; no unexpected files, keys, hooks, or processes; no private data seen returned via web/API) but cannot rule it out: a successful exploit would leave no crash or web-log trace, some attack-day logs are gone, and there was no outbound-connection logging at Alpine or its hosting provider.

Integrity checks (run Oct 24, covering Oct 20-22 commits and packages built through Oct 24): aports, packages, and the Oct 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were verified against records the attacker could not reach, a developer's clone and all 45 builders. Package/release signing keys were never stored on the GitLab server. Treated as compromised anyway; rebuilt from scratch, all passwords reset, secret keys replaced (rebuild complete Oct 28).

Alpine's own ruby package: Alpine 3.22/3.23/3.24/edge ship Ruby 3.4.12 and 3.21 ships 3.3.13, both fixed; any program compiling regexes from untrusted input is exposed, not just GitLab. Stated remediations: patch critical GitLab releases within a day and check for bundled-component patches, log outbound and DB connections, keep logs longer than 14 days, and sign release tags for GitLab-independent verification. Users of alpinelinux/gitlab must re-pull 19.3.6 (Ruby 3.3.13 image published Oct 27).
summary: Alpine Linux disclosed that on October 20-21, 2026, an attacker attempted to exploit CVE-2026-97229, a CVSS 10.0 vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates CI-configuration regular expressions whose root cause is the Onigmo regex engine bundled in Ruby. Because the fix lived in patches GitLab applies only to the Ruby in its official packages (upstream Ruby shipped it Oct 23 in 3.3.13/3.4.12/4.0.9), Alpine's instance, which used stock Ruby and had mistakenly been upgraded to 19.3.4 instead of the fixed 19.3.5, stayed vulnerable even after a later upgrade to 19.3.6. The attacker crashed GitLab workers 8 times with crafted CI configs, got partway through the exploit 4 times, and downloaded Alpine's container image to tune it. Alpine found no evidence of code execution but, lacking the logs needed to prove otherwise, treated the instance as compromised, rebuilt it from scratch, reset all passwords, and replaced secret keys. They verified aports commits, all-architecture package builds, and the October 21 stable releases against out-of-band records (a developer clone and 45 builders) and reported no tampering and no exposure of signing keys, which were never on the server. Stated remediations include faster patching, logging outbound and database connections with longer retention, and signed release tags.
novelty: detailed real-world incident response writeup, not just CVE disclosure
audience: infra/security engineers running self-hosted GitLab

title: Le Chonk: Built for Coders, Trusted by Defenders.
why: An open-weight 1T-parameter model with coding scores Mistral claims match GLM-5.3 at 47% fewer tokens per task is downloadable now from Hugging Face at $0.70/$2.10 per million input/output tokens, with weights you can self-host under a modified MIT license.
notes: Mistral Large 4 ('Le Chonk') is a 1-trillion-parameter hybrid instruct-and-reasoning MoE with multimodal input, trained from scratch on European infrastructure, supporting 160+ languages and three reasoning modes (Low/Medium/High, High is default).

Self-reported coding results: 19.7% on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0, 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (up 13pp from preview, output tokens down 30%), and 48% on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, which Mistral calls effectively tied with GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task. Surge Code blind pairwise evals ranked it behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among models tested.

Security claims: 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index (vuln discovery, reproduction, patching) and a 96.6% refusal rate on malicious cyber requests, which Mistral says is the highest it measures among open models; 97.1% resistance on the B3 Agent Security Benchmark (up from 93.3% in preview). Mistral notes it still sees 'potential for uplift to conduct real attacks' and is modifying guardrails.

A separate cybersecurity-optimized variant (pentesting, red-teaming) is in preview with partners like Orange Cyberdefense under vetted contracts restricted to authorized systems; benchmark numbers are vendor-reported with no methodology published, and a full technical report is described only as 'coming soon'.

License is the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight license (a modified MIT): free to use, modify, fine-tune, and commercialize, except Model-as-a-Service operators must obtain a separate commercial license. Priced at $0.70 input / $0.07 cached input / $2.10 output per million tokens; deployable via vLLM, SGLang, NVIDIA NIM/TensorRT-LLM, Microsoft Foundry, and OpenRouter.
Other claimed enterprise scores: 73.3% on Finch (finance/spreadsheet workflows, second to Kimi K3 among open models) and 84.5% on BrowseComp (up from a 75% SFT checkpoint).
summary: Mistral released the open weights of Mistral Large 4 ('Le Chonk'), a 1-trillion-parameter natively multimodal hybrid instruct-and-reasoning MoE trained from scratch in Europe, following three additional weeks of reinforcement learning after its public preview. Mistral claims it is the best open-weight model for coding, citing 19.7% on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0, 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 48% on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index at a claimed 47% fewer tokens than GLM-5.3. On security, it reports 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and a 96.6% refusal rate on malicious cyber requests, framing the model for defensive use while acknowledging potential uplift for real attacks and ongoing guardrail changes. The model ships with three reasoning modes, a modified-MIT 'Open-Weight' license that requires a separate commercial license only for Model-as-a-Service operators, and pricing of $0.70 input / $2.10 output per million tokens. It is available via Hugging Face, the Mistral API, OpenRouter, NVIDIA endpoints, and Microsoft Foundry; all benchmark figures are vendor-reported and the full technical report is not yet published.
novelty: open-weight 1T model leads coding/cyber benchmarks with 47% fewer tokens
audience: engineers evaluating open-weight LLMs for coding agents and defensive security tooling

title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
why: If you run Alpine's default (non-PAM) openssh-server with password auth on, anyone who can reach port 22 can log in as root or any key-only account in a single connection, no password and no CVE to track yet.
notes: The bug: sshd built without PAM hashes a login attempt with crypt() and compares it to the stored field; for accounts whose field is too short to hold a salt it borrows another account's salt. musl's crypt() returns the literal string '*' when the key exceeds 256 bytes, which is exactly what the shadow field holds for passwordless accounts, so the comparison matches and the login succeeds.

Exploit is deterministic: one connection, a single 257-to-1024-byte password, no retries. Preconditions are the name of an account whose password field is '*' (normal for key-only accounts) plus at least one local account with a $5$ or $6$ hash to supply the salt.

Affected: openssh-server (no PAM, Alpine default) or openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no, when PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default). root ships as root:* since ~3.16 but is shielded by PermitRootLogin prohibit-password unless an account can doas to root. Every checked release is affected: 3.16 through 3.24 and edge.

tiny-cloud images (qcow2/VHD/AMI) from 3.18.11 to 3.24.3 ship an 'alpine' user with field '*' and passwordless doas; safe at first boot but exploitable the moment any $6$ hash appears (admin console password, user-data hashed_passwd), yielding an alpine shell that doas-es to root.

Not affected: containers without sshd, PasswordAuthentication no, openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes, accounts locked with '!' in /etc/shadow, machines with no $-style hash, and cloud-init images (which write PasswordAuthentication no). Fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2 and backported packages (3.24: 10.3_p1-r2; 3.21: 9.9_p2-r1; down to 3.16: 9.0_p1-r6).

apk upgrade does not restart the running daemon: you must rc-service sshd restart afterward. No CVE assigned at time of writing; reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, fixed by OpenSSH's Damien Miller and Darren Tucker.
summary: Alpine Linux disclosed an unauthenticated password-authentication bypass in openssh-server built without PAM (the Alpine default), with no CVE assigned at publication. When PasswordAuthentication is yes, an attacker who knows the name of an account whose shadow field is '*' (normal for key-only accounts, including root and the cloud 'alpine' user) can log in by sending one overlong password of 257 to 1024 bytes; the attack is deterministic and needs no retries, provided at least one other local account carries a $5$ or $6$ hash. The root cause is that musl's crypt() returns the string '*' for keys over 256 bytes while sshd, lacking a salt for the passwordless account, borrows another account's salt and compares against the stored '*', producing a match. Every Alpine release checked (3.16 through 3.24 and edge) is affected, as are official tiny-cloud images, which become exploitable once any $6$ hash exists and then allow escalation to root via passwordless doas. Fixes ship in OpenSSH 10.6p2 and backported Alpine packages per branch, but apk upgrade does not restart the daemon, so sshd must be restarted manually; setting PasswordAuthentication no or using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes closes the hole otherwise. Not affected are containers without sshd, systems with password auth disabled, cloud-init images, and accounts locked with '!' in /etc/shadow.
novelty: unauthenticated auth bypass via crypt() quirk on passwordless accounts
audience: sysadmins and devops running Alpine Linux SSH servers, especially cloud/tiny-cloud images

title: Closed AI models dominate the price-performance frontier
why: If you pick models by price-per-task, the cheap open-weight option that won a third of budgets in June is now beaten almost everywhere by closed tiers like GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Haiku 5.5, leaving open weights best only at the very bottom 3% of the price range.
notes: Per Village's LLM Atlas (scores dated October 31, 2026), open-weight models are the best buy at 3% of budgets today, down from 41% in June; this is the lowest share measured, versus at least 6% at every quarter-end since 2024.

The 3% is held only at the cheap end by Google's Gemma 4 E4B and Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6-Flash; DeepSeek V4 Flash alone had won nearly a third of budgets in June, and DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp hit ~50% the week it launched in September 2025 before falling by about half or more by the next quarter.

OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna (September) and GPT-6.1 Terra (October) plus Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 retook the budgets open models held; the GPT-6/6.1 family (Luna, Terra, Sol, Astra) holds 11 of the frontier's 21 points.

Three proposed explanations: closed labs distill their own flagships into cheap tiers in-house (Haiku 5.5 followed Opus 5.5 by two weeks) while open labs' terms bar training on closed outputs; closed labs ship whole families covering every price; and they may serve inference more cheaply at scale, Google on its own chips.

Caveats stated: costs reflect what evaluators paid through hosted APIs, and open models can be cheaper on your own hardware; widening the budget window to 0.3x-10x GPT-5's cost raises today's open share back to 16% because tiny open models still win at the very cheapest end.

Methodology: capability scores derived from public benchmarks plus a separate cost model from evaluators' runs, costs normalized to GPT-5 at high effort, sampled across 201 budgets on a log scale from 1% to 3x GPT-5's cost; vendor-released model names and claims are self-reported.
summary: Village's LLM Atlas, which maps the strongest model at each price point, reports that open-weight models are now the best buy at only 3% of budgets, down from 41% in June 2026 and the lowest share it has measured since 2024. The decline followed OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Terra and Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, which undercut and out-scored the cheap DeepSeek releases (DeepSeek V4 Flash, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp) that had periodically captured wide budget bands. The post argues open wins have always come in bursts from single releases and then halved by the next quarter as closed labs shipped cheaper tiers. It offers three explanations: closed labs can distill their own frontier models into cheap tiers in-house, release full model families (GPT-6/6.1 hold 11 of 21 frontier points), and serve inference at larger scale. Caveats: costs are hosted-API prices, open models can be cheaper self-hosted, and widening the budget range to 0.3x-10x GPT-5 cost lifts the open share back to 16%. Model names and capability claims are drawn from public benchmarks and vendor releases.
novelty: open-weight share of price-performance frontier fell from 41% to 3% since June
audience: engineers/teams choosing LLMs on cost-performance tradeoffs

title: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents
why: If authentic, the archive hands any adversary a supervisor-linked org chart of 41,000 DHS staff plus named access lists for undercover programs and surveillance tools, turning spearphishing and operative-unmasking from research projects into lookups.
notes: Source and provenance: DDoSecrets published the archive as 'Icepick' on Wednesday; it and researcher maia arson crimew say a group calling itself 'Department of Peace' obtained the data from DHS's Okta login system, last updated 2026-08-19. Okta says it has no evidence its systems or data were compromised, so the breach is attributed to DHS's use of Okta, not Okta itself.

Scope (WIRED's analysis): CBP is over half the records; ICE ~10,000 (about a third in Homeland Security Investigations); USCIS 6,200; CISA ~1,000, more than half contractors. Totals cover roughly a seventh of DHS's workforce across DHS and seven component agencies.

Operational exposure: among 55,000+ permission groups, 39 HSI staff across a dozen field offices are in groups named 'CUC' (certified undercover operation); a St. Paul group references 'Keyhole,' which court filings tie to HSI surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups. Other groups name wiretap/intercept programs (Title III, CICTO, ISIP) and tools Palantir Falcon, PenLink, and the Mobile Fortify face-recognition app (200+ CBP accounts).

Access lists: identical 13-person 'Executive Leadership' and 'AI Access' groups (web-filter exceptions) include former DHS secretary Kristi Noem, ex-CIO Antoine McCord (now back at Anduril), and Philip Hegseth. Separate groups reference ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and a 'Grok.com' group of eight DHS tech officials. 700+ mostly-CBP accounts tie to a Signal-referencing group.

Legal framing: FIRE's Adam Steinbaugh argues the names and work details are 'information that would be on a business card' and cannot be criminalized, pushing back on the administration's expansive reading of 18 USC 119; crimew frames the release as accountability, not doxing.

Context and caveats: Recorded Future's Alexander Leslie calls it an 'extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource' only 'if authentic and current,' most valuable when correlated with other breach data. DHS and DOJ did not comment; the leak follows ShinyHunters' claimed theft of FBI employee data. ~1,300 ICE enforcement accounts were created after the July 4, 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act funded 10,000 new officers.
summary: DDoSecrets, working with researcher maia arson crimew, published 'Icepick,' an archive of more than 41,000 DHS employee and contractor records said to be drawn from the department's Okta login system and last updated August 19, 2026; a group calling itself 'Department of Peace' is credited with obtaining it. Per WIRED's analysis, the data spans DHS and seven component agencies—CBP (over half), ICE (~10,000), USCIS (6,200), and CISA (~1,000)—and includes emails, phone numbers, office addresses, supervisor links that allow reconstruction of reporting chains, and 55,000+ permission groups naming undercover operations (CUC, 'Keyhole'), intercept programs (Title III, CICTO, ISIP), and tools like Palantir Falcon, PenLink, and Mobile Fortify. Notable access groups include identical 13-person 'Executive Leadership' and 'AI Access' web-filter-exception lists (Kristi Noem, ex-CIO and now-Anduril Antoine McCord, Philip Hegseth) and groups referencing ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Grok. Okta says it has no evidence of compromise to its own systems. Recorded Future's Alexander Leslie calls the dataset highly valuable to adversaries 'if authentic and current,' while FIRE's Adam Steinbaugh argues the basic work details cannot be criminalized under 18 USC 119; DHS and DOJ did not comment, and the leak follows ShinyHunters' claimed theft of FBI employee data.
novelty: DHS Okta leak exposes 41K staff, undercover ops, AI tool access lists
audience: security researchers, journalists, privacy advocates tracking government surveillance infrastructure

title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
why: If you run Alpine or any musl-based system with OpenSSH built without PAM, a reachable SSH port plus a '*'-marked passwordless account means anyone can log in on the first try by pasting a 256+ character password, no credentials required.
notes: The flaw lives in the interaction between OpenSSH and musl libc (the lightweight libc alternative used by Alpine instead of glibc), and only triggers when OpenSSH is built without PAM for authentication.

Two account preconditions must both hold: at least one active user account whose password is hashed with SHA256 or SHA512, plus a target account marked passwordless with '*' in /etc/shadow (a configuration common for certificate-based auth).
Checkpoint says sshd borrows the hashed account's salt; without that salt the attack fails, and the salt-providing account must be active, not merely present as a hash.
Exploitation is a single connection with a password field longer than 256 characters: Alpine maintainers describe it as 'one connection, works every time, needs no retries.'
Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting, but accounts reachable this way that hold doas or sudo rights can still escalate to root.
Described as a decade-old bug; the article does not provide a CVE identifier, patch status, or an estimate of how many devices are affected.
summary: A roughly decade-old authentication bypass affects systems where OpenSSH is used with musl libc and without PAM, a combination common on Alpine Linux and possibly other distributions. An attacker who can reach the SSH port can log into a passwordless account (one marked '*' in /etc/shadow, as used for certificate-based auth) by supplying a password field longer than 256 characters, with no retries needed. Checkpoint researchers report that exploitation depends on the presence of an active account whose password is hashed with SHA256 or SHA512, because sshd reuses that account's salt; the attack fails without it. Alpine maintainers characterize it as reliable: 'one connection, works every time.' Root logins are protected under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting, but accounts with doas or sudo rights can still be used to escalate to root. The article does not state a CVE, patch availability, or affected-device counts.
novelty: decade-old musl+OpenSSH passwordless-account auth bypass disclosed
audience: Linux/security engineers managing Alpine or musl-based SSH deployments

title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
why: A training-free pass drops a ~58GB MoE-MLLM (InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B) onto one 40GB GPU by cutting ~27GB of expert weights, no fine-tuning required.
notes: Expert parameters dominate MoE-MLLM memory: >90% of model size, e.g. 54GB of ~58GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, despite only a few experts activating per token.

MAEP splits expert importance by modality in a single forward pass, treating text-side importance as a preservation signal and vision-side importance as the pruning signal; experts are ranked globally across layers rather than per-layer.

Two mechanisms: Delta-H Output, which measures the change in MoE output when an expert is removed (redistribution-aware), and low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side signal the authors report keeps a stable expert-importance ranking across datasets.
Claimed result: ~27GB reduction in BF16 expert weight footprint, about 47% of total memory, enough to fit a ~58GB model into a single 40GB GPU.

Evaluated on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks; authors report it beats modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks while staying competitive on text-only tasks. Code is linked.
Caveats: benchmark names, baseline identities, prune ratios, and accuracy deltas are not given in the abstract; the dataset-stability of the vision signal is asserted, not quantified here.
summary: MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning) is a training-free method for compressing Mixture-of-Experts multimodal LLMs, where expert parameters account for over 90% of model size (e.g. 54GB of ~58GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Unlike prior pruning that aggregates expert importance uniformly across tokens, MAEP decomposes importance by modality in a single forward pass: text-side importance acts as a preservation signal and vision-side importance as the pruning signal, with experts ranked globally across layers. It relies on a Delta-H Output metric (the MoE output change when an expert is removed) and on low-attention vision tokens, which the authors report give a dataset-stable importance ranking. title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
why: If you ship .NET apps, .NET 11 will refuse to start on pre-2013 x86/x64 CPUs (baseline jumps to x86-64-v2) and introduces a preview async model that moves state machines out of the compiler and into the runtime, changing what your stack traces and allocations look like.
notes: x86/x64 JIT/AOT minimum rises from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 on all OSes, now guaranteeing CX16, POPCNT, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, SSE4.2; ReadyToRun targets x86-64-v3 (adds AVX, AVX2, BMI1/2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, MOVBE) on Windows/Linux but not Apple. Older CPUs fail to launch with a 'current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets' message.

Arm64: Windows minimum now requires LSE and R2R target moves to armv8.2-a + RCPC; Linux R2R adds LSE (possible extra jitting overhead at launch); Apple M1 baseline unchanged. Microsoft frames the cut as reducing codebase maintenance complexity and matching OS-enforced hardware requirements.

Runtime Async V2 (preview, opt in via <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>) has the runtime, not the compiler, manage async suspension/resumption; the .NET runtime libraries themselves are now compiled with it and contain no compiler-generated state machines. Opt out per project with <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync>; the DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync env vars are removed. The product team asks for throughput and library-size reports rather than citing its own numbers.

Live stack traces shrink from 13 frames to 5 in the article's three-deep async example because state-machine infrastructure frames disappear; exception stack traces are unchanged. Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and R2R, reuses continuation objects, and skips saving unchanged locals.

Claimed, self-reported speedups: up to 20x for collection ops using Comparer<T>.Default/EqualityComparer<T>.Default now specialized in R2R images; up to 200x for interface-heavy code on non-JIT platforms like iOS via cached interface dispatch; ~12% faster Guid.NewGuid() on Linux using getrandom() with batch caching instead of /dev/urandom; 5-50% on Arm64 IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher workloads. None include benchmark methodology.

Written against release candidate 2. Other changes: async continuations can skip ExecutionContext capture/restore when there is nothing to restore; runtime now initializes on machines with more than 1024 logical processors (GC keeps its 1024-heap limit); in-process crash reporting via DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1; JIT bounds-check and devirtualization improvements; new SVE2/AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics and SIMD lane construction APIs.

First, minimum hardware baselines rise: x86/x64 moves from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 across Apple, Linux, and Windows, with ReadyToRun compiling for x86-64-v3 on Windows and Linux; Arm64 Windows now requires LSE and targets armv8.2-a + RCPC. Apps on unsupported older CPUs fail to start with an explicit missing-instruction-set error. Microsoft justifies the cut as reducing codebase complexity and aligning with OS-enforced requirements. Second, Runtime Async V2 (preview, opt in via <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>) relocates async suspension and resumption from compiler-generated state machines into the runtime, producing shorter live stack traces (13 frames down to 5 in the example), lower allocation pressure, and support for NativeAOT and R2R; the runtime libraries themselves are already compiled with it, and the old DOTNET_RuntimeAsync env vars are replaced by a <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> opt-out. title: The Hardest Tarball?
why: One crafted pax tarball makes 20-plus mainstream tar implementations disagree, so any system that unpacks untrusted archives has a parser-differential attack surface you can test against today.
notes: The archive is built with a single GNU tar call: pax format, delete the ?time and size fields, rename a hard link to 'café' (forcing a UTF-8 pax header), then set size=512 on that hard link whose default size is 0. 512 is exactly one tar header block, so the ambiguous bytes are the header of the following empty file.

Eight distinct extraction outcomes result. GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go, and Perl ignore the size and extract file, café, and empty correctly. bsdtar (macOS system tar) writes the 512 bytes into the hard link, so file ends up containing empty's tar header.

7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, Rust's tar, and astral-tokio-tar treat the 512 bytes as hard-link data but skip them, dropping empty. Java Commons Compress writes empty's header into a separate file; PHP PharData makes café an empty file and still extracts empty; RubyGems drops café and creates a stray PaxHeaders directory; R applies the size to empty, filling it with 512 null bytes from the end-of-archive marker.

Haskell's tar matches GNU behavior but has a string-decoding bug that writes 'cafÃ©' to disk. .NET, Julia, and uv's tar-codec reject the archive outright; the author argues rejection is the safest response even though it is not strictly POSIX-compliant.
The root ambiguity: POSIX says data blocks for a hard link 'may be included' in pax archives, leaving undefined whether a hard link can carry size and contents distinct from its original.
This is one of 134 cases in the author's haampie/tar-minefield test suite; results across implementations are tabulated at stoppels.ch/tar.
summary: A crafted tarball, buildable with a single GNU tar invocation, extracts eight different ways across well-known tar tools because it puts a pax size=512 record (one header block) on a hard-link entry whose size should be 0, exploiting undefined POSIX behavior about whether a hard link's data blocks 'may be included.' GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go, and Perl ignore the size and extract correctly; bsdtar writes the bytes into the hard link, corrupting its contents; 7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, and Rust's tar skip the data and drop the empty file; Java Commons Compress, PHP PharData, RubyGems, and R each produce their own divergent or corrupted output; Haskell's tar additionally mangles the UTF-8 filename. .NET, Julia, and uv's tar-codec reject the archive, which the author considers the safest behavior despite not being strictly POSIX-compliant. The tarball is one of 134 cases in the author's haampie/tar-minefield test suite, with a per-implementation comparison table published at stoppels.ch/tar.
novelty: crafted pax tarball extracts 8 different ways across tools
audience: systems/devtools engineers dealing with archive format edge cases and security implications

title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
why: If you were going to treat a model's self-reports of distress as evidence about its internal states, this paper shows the link is broken: a "pain" direction that flips file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% leaves no trace in what the model says.
notes: Tested three open-weight models (two Qwen models with the original pain adapters, plus one other, at 7B/8B) using Open-Weight Masked Introspection: pain and neighboring emotion directions were injected during neutral tasks, then elicited against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the model its altered words.

Across 52,920 reports (120 tasks, 4 doses, 3 prompts), pain reports never exceeded what the altered text alone revealed: exact-test bounds put the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9pp in all; Qwen2.5-32B named pain in 0 of 2,880 steered trials.

The state was clearly present internally: linear probes at the report position separated pain from sadness at 98-100% balanced accuracy, trained low-rank reporters hit 100% on held-out tasks with identical transcripts, and decodability persisted to the final layer.
Behaviorally consequential: steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% (Qwen) and from 0% to 38% (Qwen2.5-32B) with no matching verbal pain reports.

Interventions meant to restore reporting failed: injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not recover pain reports; some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer.

The pain direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person phrasing, but did not specifically track harm aimed at the model; all findings are from open-weight models with the authors' original adapters and have not been peer-reviewed.

Across 52,920 reports, pain reports never meaningfully exceeded what the altered output text alone revealed (excess below 2.5pp in 106 of 108 conditions, below 3.9pp in all), and Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials. Steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% (Qwen) and 0% to 38% (Qwen2.5-32B) without corresponding verbal reports, and attempts to restore reporting (report-token injection, removing trained denial of feelings, additional directions and readouts) failed. title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
why: Local single-stream LLM decoding is bottlenecked by streaming every weight from memory per token, and this claims a 2.52x decode speedup on a consumer RTX 4060 Ti by entropy-coding an already-quantized Llama 3.1 8B rather than just shrinking it.
notes: dtANS-LLM is a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS, exploiting weight distributions that stay non-uniform even after quantization; it exposes hyper-parameters trading compression ratio against decode cost, auto-tuned per tensor and per GPU to map a model-size vs latency Pareto front.

Self-reported results on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint: 2.52x speedup on an RTX 4060 Ti and 1.48x on an RTX 5090 over the authors' fastest baseline, at effective rates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight respectively.
The target is memory-bound single-stream decoding in local or low-latency deployments where requests cannot be batched, distinct from the server-batched regime most inference optimizations assume.

Framed as lossless compression on top of quantization; the paper claims prior lossless methods only speed up specific types like BF16 under extra assumptions, whereas MINE aims to accelerate decode generally.
Ships as a vLLM plugin that selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget, and is released open source.
Benchmarks are the authors' own with no external methodology or independent reproduction in the abstract; the arXiv ID (2611.09424) is dated beyond the current record and unverified here.
summary: MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine) is a lossless entropy-coding approach to accelerate single-stream LLM decoding, which is memory-bound because every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency settings. Its core, dtANS-LLM, is a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS that exploits non-uniform weight distributions persisting after quantization and exposes hyper-parameters trading compression ratio against decoding cost. These are auto-tuned per tensor and per GPU to obtain a Pareto front between model size and decoding latency, and the system integrates into vLLM as a plugin that selects the best kernel for a memory budget. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, the authors report 2.52x and 1.48x speedups over their fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and RTX 5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight. The work is released open source; all performance figures are self-reported in the abstract without external validation.
novelty: GPU entropy coding (dtANS-LLM) speeds single-stream LLM decoding, not just compresses
audience: engineers deploying local/low-latency LLM inference on memory-constrained GPUs

title: Halley: A Predictive Control Plane for Optical AI Data Center Networks
why: If the simulated numbers hold, a predictive control plane claims up to 3.3-14.7% less datacenter capacity to run the same frontier-model training by handling optical-network failures before they happen instead of after.
notes: Core claim: correlated laser failures, caused by lasers sharing an enclosure, cooling, and power, provably cap a pool's availability at a fixed spare ratio no matter how large the pool grows; Halley is positioned against the fixed and after-the-fact policies that run each of the optical network's four layers today.

Four components, each with a stated formal guarantee: LightReserve sizes the laser pool to a coverage bound, FoldFit schedules the switch within 11/9 of optimal, ThermaLead holds a microring with one-step-ahead control, and TriageGuard protects the highest-risk modules first; each controller defers to the deployed policy when uncertain.
Simulated effective goodput (share of ideal throughput kept) rises from 65.2% to 76.5% when a spare-exhausted window is lost, and reaches 67.4% when only dark-channel bandwidth is lost.
Reported efficiency gains: 1.03-1.17x training per megawatt, or 3.3-14.7% less datacenter capacity for the same training.
Hardware evidence: fallback circuits are formally verified, meet close timing on a commercial FPGA, and pass a 130 nm signoff; the goodput figures come from simulation, not deployment.
Surfaced on Hugging Face Daily Papers (33 points) and arXiv cs.DC; all performance numbers are authors' self-reported simulation results.
summary: Halley is a proposed predictive control plane for the optical networks that connect accelerators in frontier-AI training clusters, where each training step ends with all accelerators exchanging data at once. The paper argues that today's optical stack runs fixed or reactive policies across four layers (lasers to switches), and that correlated laser failures from shared enclosure, cooling, and power provably cap a pool's availability at any fixed spare ratio regardless of size. Halley adds a predictive controller to each layer that reads a resource's next state and acts before failure, with four components carrying formal guarantees: LightReserve (laser-pool coverage bound), FoldFit (switch scheduling within 11/9 of optimal), ThermaLead (one-step-ahead microring thermal control), and TriageGuard (highest-risk-first protection), each deferring to the deployed policy when unsure. In simulation, effective goodput rises from 65.2% to 76.5% when a spare-exhausted window is lost and reaches 67.4% when only dark-channel bandwidth is lost, which the authors translate to 1.03-1.17x training per megawatt or 3.3-14.7% less datacenter capacity for the same training. The fallback circuits are formally verified, meet close timing on a commercial FPGA, and pass a 130 nm signoff. All throughput numbers are self-reported simulation results rather than production measurements.
novelty: predictive, pre-failure control plane for optical DC networks vs reactive policies
audience: datacenter/networking engineers building large-scale AI training infrastructure

title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
why: If you manage or hope to land a junior engineering role, note that the company most aggressively building its workflow around AI cut junior technical hires from 27% to 9% of hires since early 2025.
notes: Junior-level staff in technical departments fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025; junior technical hires dropped more steeply, from 27% to 9%. All figures are self-reported by Anthropic.
Technical teams fell from 61% to 56% of the overall workforce, which Anthropic attributes partly to coding tools letting non-technical employees build software themselves.

An April 2026 internal survey found 27% of employees felt more productive because of Claude, while 20% said their job had shifted from doing work to 'managing Claudes'; one engineer likened it to babysitting.
The report calls human attention and judgment the new productivity bottleneck as Claude produces a 'deluge' of text to read and organize.
Meeting time per employee is up 20% year-over-year (16% for technical contributors), which Anthropic ties to 'human trust and accountability' and face-to-face coordination described as indispensable.

Anthropic claims more output per person (more code, more sales closed, more contracts processed) and says it has found no sign of declining code quality, while conceding more code is not necessarily better code. No external methodology or data is provided.
summary: A report Anthropic published on October 17, 2026 details how its own workforce and work patterns changed over the prior year as it molded workflows around Claude. Self-reported figures show junior-level employees in technical departments fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025, with junior technical hires dropping from 27% to 9%, and technical teams shrinking from 61% to 56% of the overall workforce. An April 2026 survey found 27% of employees felt more productive with Claude and 20% said their job had shifted to 'managing Claudes,' with the report framing human attention and judgment as the new bottleneck as Claude output grows. Meeting time per employee rose 20% year-over-year (16% for technical staff), which Anthropic attributes to the need for human trust and face-to-face coordination. The company claims higher output per person and no detected decline in code quality, while acknowledging more code does not mean better code. Anthropic positions these internal trends as a possible early indicator of broader AI-driven shifts in hiring and labor demand, though it offers no external benchmark or methodology.
novelty: Anthropic's own internal labor-market data on AI-driven org change
audience: AI leaders and managers thinking about org design under heavy AI adoption

title: Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
why: If your team pasted passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI, Notion says to rotate them now: those chat transcripts sat on breached infrastructure at inference vendor Fireworks AI.
notes: Fireworks AI, used by Notion as a general inference provider for open-weight models and for classification jobs behind the Insights feature, was breached; Fireworks notified Notion on Nov 6 that malicious actors may have accessed customer data, and confirmed the dataset on Nov 8.

Notion's security team says fewer than 1% of workspaces may be affected. The exposed data is 'unattributable' Notion AI chat transcripts: not labeled with author or workspace, and containing no tool call results (no Notion page content or external data pulled in by the AI).

Notion says it disconnected from Fireworks, deleted all data in Fireworks' systems, stopped all traffic, and halted all training runs as of Nov 3; the Insights feature is disabled and open-weight models are no longer served through Fireworks.
Notion tells affected teams to treat the chat data as exposed and rotate any credentials pasted into Notion AI during the window. Caveat: it gives no specific exposure dates for the window.

Affected Enterprise workspace owners can pull a CSV plus an annotated CSV with added user-attribution metadata (marked __metadata / __analysis) that Notion says was NOT part of the exposure; data is viewable only via desktop or web, not mobile.
Fireworks is described, by Notion, as serving tens of thousands of customers and hundreds of thousands of developers; the breach is Fireworks' own, with Notion as a downstream customer.
summary: Notion disclosed a security incident at Fireworks AI, a third-party inference vendor it used to serve open-weight models and to run classification jobs for its Insights feature. Fireworks notified Notion on Nov 6 that malicious actors may have accessed customer data and confirmed the dataset on Nov 8; Notion's investigation found that fewer than 1% of its workspaces may be affected, with exposure limited to 'unattributable' Notion AI chat transcripts that lacked author/workspace labels and tool call results. Notion says it disconnected from Fireworks, deleted its data there, stopped all traffic, and halted training runs as of Nov 3, and has disabled Insights. It has contacted affected workspace owners, who can retrieve the affected data (Enterprise owners get both a raw CSV and an annotated CSV with user-attribution metadata that Notion says was not itself exposed). Notion recommends treating the chat data as exposed and rotating any passwords, API keys, or credentials pasted into Notion AI during the period, though it does not specify exact exposure dates.
novelty: third-party AI vendor breach exposes unattributable Notion AI chat logs
audience: security engineers and teams evaluating third-party AI inference vendor risk

title: Your TV can see through walls
why: A passive receiver and a nearby broadcast tower are enough to detect and estimate the speed of someone walking in another room, with no transmitter of your own and no cooperation from the target.
notes: The effect is selective fading: the direct TV signal is partially canceled by a strong reflection, and because the reflection's phase depends on frequency, the cancellation is uneven across the band and extremely sensitive to nearby motion.
Each dark stripe in the waterfall marks the reflected path changing length by one wavelength as the author's body moves, so counting stripe spacing yields Doppler-like motion data.
Worked example: stripe spacing ~70 pixels at a 150 Hz waterfall update rate gives 0.47 s per stripe (2.1 Hz); at 490 MHz that resolves to ~1.3 m/s, or 4.6 km/h walking speed.
Motion was perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the derived speed needs no geometric correction; off-axis motion would require adjustment.
The author claims any wideband signal (WiFi, LTE, broadcast TV) works the same way, but says WiFi and LTE produce messier waterfalls that need more processing to extract the same data.
Caveat: this is a single hobbyist demonstration with spectrogram screenshots, not a calibrated or peer-reviewed measurement; sensitivity, range, and target discrimination are not characterized.
summary: The author shows that a simple RF receiver watching a local TV broadcast can detect human motion through walls by observing selective fading, where a reflected copy of the direct signal cancels it unevenly across frequency. Small movements, such as standing up or a few centimeters of antenna shift, visibly disturb the fading pattern, and walking in a neighboring room produces regular stripes in the waterfall. Each stripe corresponds to the reflected path length changing by one wavelength, so the author derives walking speed from stripe spacing (~70 pixels), the waterfall update rate (150 Hz), and the carrier frequency (490 MHz), arriving at about 1.3 m/s or 4.6 km/h. Because the motion was perpendicular to the signal path, no geometric correction was needed. The author argues the same passive technique generalizes to any wideband signal including WiFi and LTE, though those sources produce messier waterfalls requiring more processing. The piece is an informal demonstration illustrated with spectrograms rather than a rigorous study, and it does not quantify range, resolution, or reliability.
novelty: quantifying passive RF motion sensing via selective fading from TV broadcast signals
audience: security researchers and RF/SDR hobbyists interested in passive sensing and surveillance implications

title: ClickHouse Acquires Xata
why: If you run a branch-per-PR or branch-per-agent-run workflow, the Postgres copy-on-write tech that makes ~3-second branches on multi-TB databases is now headed into ClickHouse Managed Postgres, with an agentic tier and scale-to-zero planned.
notes: Xata claims copy-on-write branching creates a branch in ~3 seconds even on multi-terabyte databases, with billing on the diff: the post says 50 branches of a 1TB database cost closer to 1TB than 50TB. Child branches get independent compute on a separate physical node.
Scale-to-zero suspends idle databases and wakes them on the next connection in ~1 second; combined with branching, this is pitched for per-PR, per-agent-run, or per-SQL-session databases.

Mechanism: Xatastor storage engine separates storage and compute by exposing ZFS zvols over NVMe/TCP at the block-device level, so unmodified vanilla Postgres runs on top; warm pools of compute instances keep node/pod provisioning off the hot path. Xata also maintains open-source pgstream (replication with anonymization) and pgroll (reversible schema changes).

ClickHouse Managed Postgres runs on local NVMe, reached GA the same day, and is claimed by ClickHouse to be the fastest Postgres service; both it and Xata run vanilla Postgres. The David AI testimonial (claiming a move off Neon) is a customer quote, not independent benchmarking.

Transition: nothing changes for Xata customers short-term and sign-ups continue, but Xata customers will eventually be migrated to ClickHouse Managed Postgres once branching, scale-to-zero, and an agentic tier reach feature parity there. No price, timeline, or deal terms disclosed.
Named AI-native customers (Sapien, Enginy, David AI, Runner AI, LoopAI) are each said to create thousands of branches weekly; these are self-reported usage figures without methodology.
summary: Xata is joining ClickHouse to fold its instant Postgres provisioning, copy-on-write branching, and scale-to-zero compute into ClickHouse Managed Postgres, which reached GA the same day on local NVMe storage. Xata claims branches on multi-terabyte databases are created in about 3 seconds while billing only for the diff, and that idle databases scale to zero and wake in roughly 1 second. The technology rests on the Xatastor storage engine, which exposes ZFS zvols over NVMe/TCP at the block-device level to run unmodified vanilla Postgres, plus warm pools of compute instances to keep provisioning off the hot path. The companies frame the combination as best-in-class OLTP (Postgres) plus OLAP (ClickHouse), targeting branch-per-PR and per-agent-run workflows; named AI customers are claimed to create thousands of branches weekly. Xata will keep operating and accepting sign-ups short-term, but its customers will eventually be migrated to ClickHouse Managed Postgres once feature parity is reached. No deal terms, pricing, or timeline are disclosed, and performance and customer claims are vendor-reported.
novelty: Xata's Postgres branching tech folded into ClickHouse Managed Postgres
audience: devs building AI coding agents/CI pipelines needing ephemeral databases

title: Horible public key tricks
why: A CA will sign a certificate whose RSA modulus spells out a human-readable message, so the "random" public key in a trusted cert is attacker-controllable to the bit and worth remembering next time you reason about what a CA actually validates.
notes: Method: pick two random primes, compute n, overwrite bytes in n's upper half to embed an ASCII message in its base64 encoding, then restore a valid factorization by setting q to the next prime after n/p. Because p and q are close in size, incrementing q only perturbs the lower half of the product, leaving the message in the top half intact.

The CA (Let's Encrypt, per the pasted cert) refuses non-standard public exponents, so e stays 65537 (0x10001); only the modulus is used as the message carrier. The author embedded text including 'No one checks these things' and a jab at a CA that 'got away with the number 4 for a year.'

Capacity is roughly 150 characters for RSA-2048 and 320 for RSA-4096 in base64; targeting the hex view browsers show would roughly double density (2 chars/byte vs 0.75) but constrains word choice. Base64's 3-byte grouping can misalign the message, fixable in under 4 placement attempts since the cert layout is static.

Self-reported security caveats: the technique lowers private-key entropy; the script does not check for insecure outputs such as p and q too close together (enabling Fermat-style factoring) or a very small d. Author argues the cert is still fine for a public site because modern TLS forward secrecy means a leaked key alone does not enable passive decryption, only active MITM.

Framed as a 'protest certificate' against the ACME/expiry treadmill rather than a real alternative to PKI; author concedes such modulus-fixing tricks were studied as RSA compression (fixing up to 2/3 of n for 1/3 size) but largely abandoned for cryptosystems that natively use small keys.
summary: The author demonstrates encoding a readable ASCII message into the RSA modulus of a valid, CA-signed TLS certificate. Starting from two random primes, they overwrite bytes in the upper half of the modulus n to inject text into its base64 representation, then repair the factorization by replacing q with the next prime above n/p; since p and q are similar in size, this only disturbs the lower half of the product and leaves the message intact. The public exponent is kept at 65537 because the CA (Let's Encrypt, per the included certificate) rejects non-standard exponents. Usable capacity is about 150 characters at RSA-2048 and 320 at RSA-4096, with a hex-targeted variant offering more room; base64 alignment issues are resolved in under four attempts. The piece is framed as a protest against ACME complexity and short certificate lifetimes, and against CA practices, citing an incident where a CA used the modulus value 4 for a year. The author notes the method reduces key entropy and that their script does not guard against insecure outputs (close primes allowing factoring, or small d), but argues TLS forward secrecy keeps a public website safe from passive eavesdropping even if the key is weak.
novelty: embedding ASCII protest message inside RSA modulus of a valid CA-signed cert
audience: security engineers and crypto/PKI tinkerers
